notes: Local eateries, market traders and small cafes mostly prefer cash, and card payment may not be accepted everywhere, so keep some small change on you.
On municipal buses between Cunda, Sarımsaklı and Küçükköy the Balkart is practical, but paying cash on dolmuşes is also common.

In July the sun is very strong between 12:00 and 16:00; a hat, sunscreen and plenty of water are essential for the beach and outdoor sightseeing, and if possible take a break in the shade during the hot hours.
In historic buildings such as Taksiyarhis Church and the Rahmi M. Koç Museum, it is local etiquette not to talk loudly and to follow the photography rules.
In fish restaurants and meyhanes, a tip of about 5-10% of the bill is left in cash; some venues add a service charge to the bill automatically, so check first.
Ayvalık does not have nightlife as lively as Bodrum or Çeşme; a calm holiday-town feel prevails, so plan accordingly.
When buying olive oil, olives and soap, especially at neighbourhood markets and in Küçükköy, polite haggling is considered normal.

niche.name: Yeşil Koy
niche.why_hidden: This cove on the south coast of Cunda Island is sometimes visited by boat tours, but with no road or signposts, most visitors don't know it. Those who know it can be reached on foot via the olive grove path are usually locals who know the island well or returning travellers.
niche.access_instructions: From central Cunda it is about a 40-minute walk along the path through the olive groves, and there are no signs; if you ask the fishermen in Cunda for the path to Yeşil Koy, they will point you in the right direction. Alternatively, you can go by a small boat rented for the day from Cunda pier.
niche.local_contact: Yok — resmi bir işletme veya rehber yok; Cunda iskelesindeki balıkçılardan biriyle günlük kayık anlaşması yapılabilir.
niche.season: May-October (in summer the sea is warm and calm; in winter the path is poorly maintained and deserted)
niche.insider_tip: Bring water, snacks and sun protection, as the cove has no kiosk or facilities. If the return walk feels tiring, you can ask one of the fishermen at the pier to take you back by boat for a few hundred lira.
niche.show_reason: Cunda'nın turist otobüslerinin hiç uğramadığı, tamamen zeytinlik patikasını bilenlerin ulaştığı bakir bir koy — ücretsiz ve fotojenik ama erişimi yerel bilgi gerektiriyor.
niche.address: Cunda (Alibey) Adası güney kıyısı, Ayvalık Adaları Tabiat Parkı sınırı, Ayvalık, Balıkesir

transit.name: Balkart
transit.why_chosen: Balkart is the single card valid on all municipal buses run by Balıkesir Metropolitan Municipality, and it covers the lines linking central Ayvalık with Cunda, Sarımsaklı, Küçükköy and Altınova, so you can pay for most of the planned daily neighbourhood transfers with one card. Cash is also accepted on dolmuşes, but on the municipal buses, which run more often in the summer season, Balkart is both faster and cheaper.

days.theme: Cunda's stone lanes, a hidden cove and Greek cuisine

stops.name: Cunda Fishing Harbour Morning Market
stops.tips: Boats return early in the morning with the day's catch, and wandering the harbour shows you Cunda's real morning rhythm. Strike up a chat with the fishermen about the day's bluefish or sea bream, and ask where to buy for dinner.

stops.name: Taksiyarhis Church
stops.tips: This 19th-century Greek church now hosts art exhibitions, and entry is by donation. Don't miss the iconostasis remnants and the ceiling frescoes inside.

stops.name: Bay Nihat
stops.tips: One of the island's longest-established fish restaurants, with a warm, unpretentious table. Ask for the seasonal fish and the olive-oil sea beans (deniz börülcesi); the queue is shorter at lunchtime.

stops.name: Yeşil Koy
stops.tips: One of the island's most unspoilt coves, reached by a 40-minute path through olive groves from central Cunda. Bring water and sun protection, as there is no kiosk at the cove; on the way back, ask the fishermen at the pier whether they can take you back by boat.

stops.name: Yakamoz Avlu Restaurant
stops.tips: A family-run restaurant in a Greek house dating from 1882, where dinner in the courtyard is a treat. Ask for a selection of shrimp casserole and seasonal meze; booking is recommended.

stops.name: Cunda Square
stops.tips: Take an evening stroll through the stone lanes and pick up mastic ice cream from the shops on the square. On summer evenings the square stays lively until late.

backups.name: Deniz Restaurant
backups.tips: One of the classic fish restaurants lining the Cunda waterfront, with sea-view tables for a lunchtime catch. The grilled octopus and artichokes in olive oil are recommended.

backups.name: Cunda Windmills
backups.tips: The remains of historic windmills on the island's hilltop are ideal for photos near sunset. Entry is free, and you can get there on foot or by a short taxi ride.

days.theme: Ayvalık's iconic sunset rocks and golden beach

stops.name: Cennet Tepesi
stops.tips: At the municipal hilltop cafe, enjoy the view over Cunda and the Kaz Mountains with an Ayvalık toast and tea; toast prices are quite reasonable. The morning light is clearer and the crowds are thinner.

stops.name: Devil's Table
stops.tips: Entry is free, and only those arriving by car pay a parking fee. See the legendary footprint and the views of the islands from the rocks. There is little shade at midday, so bring a hat.

stops.name: Paşa Çorba
stops.tips: A local eatery known for its daily olive-oil dishes and home cooking. Depending on the season, try the stuffed okra or stuffed zucchini flowers, and don't miss the soups.

stops.name: Sarımsaklı Beach
stops.tips: Ayvalık's famous 7 km golden beach has shallow, warm water, so you can swim for a long time. Sunbed prices vary by area and you can rent them from the facilities on the shore.

stops.name: Deniz Yıldızı
stops.tips: A small local eatery famous for its soup, worth the wait even if there is a queue at the door. In artichoke season, try the artichokes in olive oil and the mastic cookies.

stops.name: Sarımsaklı Seafront
stops.tips: Take a lit evening walk along the shore in the cool air; the ice cream shops stay open late. The benches by the sea are an ideal spot to sit and end the day.

backups.name: Paşşalı Müdavim Çorbacısı
backups.tips: A calm local eatery serving soups and home cooking that its regulars love. Around 13:00 is the most relaxed time to go, and the daily menu is written on a board.

backups.name: Lale Island Viewpoint
backups.tips: The small island right next to the bridge between Ayvalık and Cunda is a favourite with photographers for its olive-covered hills and clear sea. It makes a good short stop on the way, and entry is free.

days.theme: Stone lanes, olive oil heritage and market bustle

stops.name: Ayvalık Historic Greek Streets (Barbaros and Talatpaşa Neighbourhoods)
stops.tips: A free walking route: in the narrow, honeysuckle-scented lanes, look at the stone and timber houses dating from the 1700s. Morning light shows off the facades best, so take your coffee break in these streets.

stops.name: Ayvalık Rahmi M. Koç Museum
stops.tips: A restored 200-year-old olive oil factory that explains the steam engines and the production line. Closed on Mondays; open to visitors 10:00-17:00.

stops.name: Fırat Lokantası
stops.tips: A small local eatery that has been serving since 1988. Choose one of the daily home-cooked dishes; going around 13:30 makes it easier to find a table.

stops.name: Ayvalık Olive Oil Tasting Tour
stops.tips: A guided tasting tour in a boutique producer's workshop, following the olive's journey from harvest to bottle. You taste oils from different harvest periods, and advance booking is required.

stops.name: Ayvalık Central Neighbourhood Market
stops.tips: The central Ayvalık market is held every Thursday, and if you land on that day you will be amazed by the variety of olives, cheese and local herbs. A smile helps when you haggle.

stops.name: Papaz'ın Evi
stops.tips: Right next to the Rahmi Koç Museum, it offers the atmosphere of a Greek meyhane (tavern) with a garden. Starting with fava and sea beans and moving on to the seasonal fish is the classic route.

backups.name: Tik Mustafa'nın Yeri
backups.tips: Open all year round, it is one of the best-loved addresses for rakı and local meze culture. You can choose from nearly 30 meze, and going early in the late afternoon improves your chances of a table.

backups.name: Ayvalık Ayazma (Panagia Phaneromeni)
backups.tips: A little-known Greek holy spring with a calm, shaded courtyard. It rarely appears in guidebooks, and it is a good alternative for those who want to explore the historic fabric quietly.

days.theme: Küçükköy's art lanes and a quiet local beach

stops.name: Küçükköy Art Galleries (Artura Gallery, KıraARThane)
stops.tips: In Küçükköy, a former Bosnian village, restored stone houses have become 32 art galleries. Walking along the cobbled lanes, you come across a different ceramics or painting studio at every corner, and entry is mostly free.

stops.name: Majka
stops.tips: A calm cafe serving an Aegean breakfast alongside Bosnian pastry (börek) with olive oil. It is most enjoyable at the point where late breakfast meets early lunch.

stops.name: Badavut Beach
stops.tips: West of Sarımsaklı, a quiet beach about 2 km long, away from the crowds. Sunbed options are not as plentiful as at Sarımsaklı, so it is best to arrive early and claim a spot.

stops.name: Zeljanik
stops.tips: One of Küçükköy's small restaurants with a Bosnian-Balkan flavour, known for its homemade pies. It is usually best to order whatever is on the evening menu.

stops.name: Küçükköy Square
stops.tips: Have one last coffee at the cafes on the square, the village's social centre. The night lighting gives the stone houses a different atmosphere.

backups.name: Kürşat Zeytin Evi Restaurant
backups.tips: An olive-themed local eatery on the Izmir-Çanakkale road. Try the olive paste and the stuffed vine leaves in olive oil; it has a quiet garden.

backups.name: Patriça Bay
backups.tips: A historic cove north of Cunda, known for its shallow, clear water. You reach it from Küçükköy by small boat, and you need to agree a daily price with local boat owners.

days.theme: Boat trip around Ayvalık Islands' coves and nightlife

stops.name: Başka Cafe
stops.tips: Known as the number one address for Ayvalık toast, it is ideal for a light breakfast before boarding the boat. Plain toast and fresh orange juice is the classic combination.

stops.name: Ayvalık Islands Boat Tour (12 Islands)
stops.tips: In the clear waters around Ayvalık's 24 islands, the tour gives you an hour-long swimming break in each of three different coves. Lunch is fish or chicken schnitzel, and don't forget sunscreen and swimwear.

stops.name: Mithra Restaurant
stops.tips: Set in an old factory building, it offers dinner with live music and sea views. It is best to start with meze and move on to the seasonal fish; booking is recommended.

stops.name: Zuzu Cafe Bar
stops.tips: One of the rare venues in Ayvalık with a live music programme in both summer and winter. It suits a last stop of the day with a cold beer, and it is busier at weekends.

backups.name: Ayna
backups.tips: A venue on Cunda Island that brings together Mediterranean and Cretan cooking. The standout plates are the prawn pasta with rocket and the sardines in vine leaves.

backups.name: Ayia Yorgi Church
backups.tips: One of the historic churches on Cunda visited on boat tours, with a simple, quiet atmosphere. Entry is free, and it suits a short stop depending on the tour schedule.

stops.name: Acropolis of Pergamon
stops.tips: The journey from Ayvalık takes about 50 minutes, and you can go by dolmuş (shared minibus) or private car. Taking the cable car up the hill is both scenic and quick, and from here you can see the steepest theatre of the ancient world.

stops.name: Asklepion
stops.tips: One of Anatolia's first medical and healing centres, so don't miss the sacred way and its tunnel. From April to October it is open to visitors 08:00-19:00.

stops.name: Bergama Sofrası
stops.tips: A casual, friendly local eatery on the street leading to the Hacı Hekim Hamam. Don't leave without trying Bergama kavurma (braised meat).

stops.name: Red Basilica
stops.tips: This huge brick structure, also known as the Temple of Serapis, is impressive for its underground tunnels. It is open 08:30-20:00, and the afternoon light is better for photos.

stops.name: Bergama Bazaar (Coppersmiths' Street)
stops.tips: A good place for one last stroll before heading back, with haggling possible in the coppersmith and carpet shops. You can also find local dried fruit and spices here.

backups.name: Altın Kepçe Bergama Köfte
backups.tips: A local eatery serving since 1975, also known for its morning soups. Köfte (grilled meatballs) and roasted peppers are the classic pair.

backups.name: Bergama Archaeology Museum
backups.tips: It houses the smaller finds and statues from the archaeological sites, and is far less crowded than the sites themselves. It is also a good alternative for a rainy day.

days.theme: A quiet Ayvalık morning before leaving

stops.name: Ortunç Bay
stops.tips: Cunda's only Blue Flag beach lies within national park boundaries, so you have forest behind you and the sea in front. It is not crowded early in the morning, which makes it ideal for a last swim.

stops.name: Cunda Pier Viewpoint
stops.tips: For a short farewell photo stop, the area around the pier shows both the boats and the open sea. The morning light is quite good for photos.

stops.name: Tamam
stops.tips: It takes a creative approach to Turkish meze, and its long meze list suits a light farewell lunch. The standout plates are the borlotti beans with cinnamon and the sea beans.

stops.name: Ayvalık Bazaar (olive oil and soap shopping)
stops.tips: The last stop for buying Ayvalık olive oil and olive oil soap before you leave. Check the label to make sure you are buying geographically indicated Ayvalık olive oil.

backups.name: Lal Girit Mutfağı
backups.tips: It serves dishes such as oven-roasted lamb shank with thyme and Cretan-style black-eyed beans. A good alternative for anyone after a light but filling farewell lunch.

backups.name: Çınarlı Mosque (Agia Iorgi Church)
backups.tips: A historic mosque on Cunda, formerly a church, built in 1880. It suits a short break in the shade of century-old plane trees, and entry is free.
